section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About HER2-Positive Gastric Cancer
section.intro: Clear, patient-friendly answers about HER2-positive gastric cancer, including how trastuzumab and T-DXd work, and what treatment access in China may involve for international patients.

items.a: HER2-positive gastric cancer is a stomach cancer in which tumour cells make too much of a protein called HER2, which can drive faster growth. This subtype is confirmed through laboratory testing of a tissue sample and is found in a portion of gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction cancers. Identifying HER2 status matters because it may allow the use of HER2-targeted treatments, which should always be selected by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: How is HER2 status tested in gastric cancer?
items.a: HER2 status in gastric cancer is tested on a biopsy or surgical tissue sample using immunohistochemistry (IHC) and, when needed, in-situ hybridisation (ISH or FISH). IHC scores protein levels from 0 to 3+, and borderline results are confirmed with ISH to check for extra HER2 gene copies. Accurate testing depends on adequate tissue and experienced pathology review, so results should be interpreted alongside the full diagnosis by the treating specialist.

items.q: What is trastuzumab and how does it work?
items.a: Trastuzumab is a targeted antibody medicine that attaches to the HER2 protein on cancer cells and helps slow their growth. In HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer, it is generally combined with chemotherapy as a first-line option for suitable patients. It is given by intravenous infusion over cycles. Whether trastuzumab is appropriate depends on confirmed HER2 status, cancer stage, overall health, and specialist review, and it does not guarantee a specific outcome.

Trastuzumab deruxtecan, or T-DXd, is an antibody-drug conjugate that links a HER2-targeting antibody to a chemotherapy payload, delivering treatment more directly to HER2-positive cancer cells. It is studied and used in certain patients with HER2-positive gastric cancer whose disease has progressed after earlier treatment. Because it carries specific risks, T-DXd is given under close medical supervision, and eligibility should be decided by the treating oncology team after full review.

items.q: Who is eligible for trastuzumab in gastric cancer?
items.a: Trastuzumab may be considered for patients with confirmed HER2-positive advanced or metastatic gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer, usually as part of first-line therapy with chemotherapy. Eligibility depends on HER2 test results, cancer type and stage, heart function, previous treatments, and overall health. Because trastuzumab can affect the heart, baseline checks are often done first. Final decisions on suitability should be made by a qualified oncology team after reviewing the complete case.

items.q: When is T-DXd used in HER2-positive gastric cancer?
items.a: T-DXd is generally considered for HER2-positive gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer that has progressed after a prior trastuzumab-based regimen. It is used as a later-line option in selected patients rather than as an initial treatment. Because responses and risks vary, treatment requires confirmed HER2 status and careful monitoring. Whether T-DXd is appropriate depends on previous therapy, current health, and specialist assessment, and outcomes cannot be guaranteed for any individual patient.

items.q: What are the side effects of trastuzumab?
items.a: Common side effects of trastuzumab can include infusion reactions, fever, chills, tiredness, and, less often, effects on heart function. Because it may weaken the heart's pumping strength, doctors usually check heart function before and during treatment. When combined with chemotherapy, additional side effects from those drugs may occur. Side effects vary from person to person, and any new or worsening symptoms should be reported promptly to the treating medical team for proper management.

items.q: What are the risks of T-DXd?
items.a: T-DXd can cause side effects such as nausea, fatigue, low blood counts, and hair changes, and it carries a specific risk of lung inflammation called interstitial lung disease, which can be serious. For this reason, patients are monitored closely, and new breathing symptoms should be reported immediately. Heart function may also be checked. Because these risks require careful oversight, T-DXd should only be given and managed by an experienced oncology team.

items.q: How much does HER2-targeted treatment for gastric cancer cost?
items.a: The cost of HER2-targeted treatment varies widely and cannot be quoted as a fixed figure. It depends on the specific drug, number of cycles, hospital, country, accompanying chemotherapy, tests, and any complications or hospital stays. Trastuzumab and T-DXd differ in price, and biosimilar versions of trastuzumab may lower cost in some regions. A reliable estimate should be based on the confirmed treatment plan and advice from the treating team.

Trastuzumab is available in China and is used for eligible patients with HER2-positive cancers, including gastric cancer, at many major hospitals. Both the originator medicine and biosimilar versions may be accessible, which can affect pricing. Availability at a specific hospital, and whether it fits a particular patient, still depends on confirmed HER2 status, medical review, and local supply. Treatment decisions and access are determined by the treating oncology team after full assessment.

items.q: Is T-DXd approved and accessible in China?
items.a: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has become accessible in China for certain HER2-positive cancers, though its availability and approved uses can change over time and vary by hospital. Access for gastric cancer depends on regulatory status, hospital supply, and whether the patient meets clinical criteria. Because approvals and stock may differ between centres, patients should confirm current availability and suitability directly with the treating hospital and oncology team before making plans.

items.q: Are trastuzumab biosimilars available for gastric cancer?
items.a: Biosimilar versions of trastuzumab are available in several countries, including China and India, and may be used for eligible HER2-positive gastric cancer patients. A biosimilar is a closely comparable version of the original biologic medicine reviewed by regulators for similar quality and effect. Biosimilars can help reduce treatment cost, but whether one is suitable, and which product is used, depends on hospital availability and the treating oncology team's clinical judgement.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for HER2-positive gastric cancer in China?
items.a: China runs a number of clinical trials exploring HER2-targeted therapies, antibody-drug conjugates, and combinations for gastric cancer, and some international patients have taken part. Enrollment is never guaranteed and is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment. Trials have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria based on HER2 status, prior treatment, and overall health. Interested patients should discuss trial options and current openings with their oncology team before applying.

items.q: What happens if HER2-positive gastric cancer stops responding to trastuzumab?
items.a: If HER2-positive gastric cancer progresses after trastuzumab-based treatment, other options may be considered, including T-DXd, different chemotherapy regimens, or a suitable clinical trial. Doctors may also repeat testing to reassess HER2 status and guide next steps. The best option depends on previous treatments, current health, and specialist review. Because each situation is different, the choice of further therapy should always be made by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Are newer HER2 therapies being studied for gastric cancer?
items.a: Researchers are studying newer HER2-directed approaches for gastric cancer, including next-generation antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, and combinations with immunotherapy. Some of these are being evaluated in trials in China and elsewhere, but many remain investigational and are not standard care. Availability and suitability depend on trial access, confirmed HER2 status, and medical review. Patients interested in emerging options should discuss them, and their risks, with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to explore treatment abroad?
items.a: To explore HER2-positive gastric cancer treatment abroad, hospitals usually need recent pathology and biopsy reports, HER2 test results (IHC and ISH where done), imaging scans such as CT or PET-CT, endoscopy findings, blood tests, and a summary of previous treatments. Organised, up-to-date records help doctors give an accurate opinion. Requirements can vary by hospital, and the treating team abroad decides what additional tests or repeat testing may be needed.

items.q: How can international patients access gastric cancer treatment in China?
items.a: International patients can seek HER2-positive gastric cancer treatment in China by sending medical records to a chosen hospital for review, obtaining a treatment plan and estimate, and then arranging travel and a medical visa. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Confirming details early with the hospital helps patients plan realistically and safely.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with HER2-positive gastric cancer?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. It can also help patients explore whether options such as trastuzumab, T-DXd, or clinical trials may be relevant to discuss. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, HER2 status, previous treatment, and overall health.
